job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
For our explainer ahead of next Thursday's markup, we want to cover the bill's weak spots. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Based solely on the supplied text, these are potential loopholes, ambiguities, and enforcement problems—not conclusions that a court would invalidate the bill. Some omissions could be addressed by existing law, but the text does not specify how.

### Definitions and scope

1. **§ 2(1)(A)—Per-vessel threshold permits fragmentation.** The definition measures recovery by “a single vessel,” rather than aggregating recovery across an operator, corporate group, or project. Companies could spread extraction among vessels that each recover no more than 10,000 metric tons annually, although the discretionary catchall in § 2(1)(B) could potentially reach those activities.

2. **§ 2(1)(A)—Exact quantity and depth cutoffs.** Recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons per year, or recovery at exactly 200 meters or shallower, falls outside subparagraph (A). Those operations would require a separate basis for coverage under subparagraph (B).

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—Undefined annual accounting period.** “Per year” does not specify a calendar year, rolling 12-month period, or annualized production rate. This creates uncertainty about split-year operations and when an operation crosses the threshold.

4. **§§ 2(1)(A), 5(a)—Unclear violation days for threshold-based mining.** The bill does not say whether exceeding the annual threshold makes earlier recovery days unlawful, or whether liability begins only when the threshold is exceeded. That matters substantially for penalties of up to $1 million per day.

5. **§ 2(1)(A)—Undefined measurement rules.** The text does not specify whether tonnage means dry minerals, wet nodules, or material including sediment, nor where depth is measured. Different measurement methods could change whether an operation qualifies.

6. **§ 2(1)(A)—Unclear meaning and attribution of “recovery.”** The bill does not say whether recovery occurs at seabed collection, lifting, or delivery aboard a vessel, or how to attribute production involving several vessels or subsea systems. This could invite disputes over which vessel crosses the threshold and whether non-vessel extraction systems fall within subparagraph (A).

7. **§ 2(1)(B)—Undefined decision-maker.** “The Secretary” is never defined; the separate reference to the Secretary of State in § 6 does not clearly assign this environmental determination power. That leaves uncertainty over who can expand coverage beyond the numerical definition.

8. **§ 2(1)(B)—Unbounded comparable-risk standard.** The catchall specifies no risk metrics, comparison methodology, or sufficiently precise reference operation, and “any activity” is not expressly limited to mineral extraction. This invites disputes over statutory scope, fair notice, and the justification for particular determinations, especially where criminal liability follows.

9. **§ 2(1)(B)—No determination process or deadline.** The text does not specify whether coverage is established by regulation or individual order, what notice is required, or when a determination takes effect. Operators below the numerical threshold could continue while determinations remain unmade and contest penalties imposed without adequate prior notice.

10. **§ 2(2)—Incomplete coverage of domestic entities.** “U.S. person” includes citizens and state-organized corporations but does not expressly include LLCs, partnerships, trusts, or federally, territorially, or District of Columbia-organized entities. Those omissions create arguments against coverage of their overseas activities, even though conduct within the United States remains covered.

11. **§§ 2(2), 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries and noncitizen residents.** The definition does not include foreign-incorporated subsidiaries merely because Americans own or control them, or noncitizen U.S. residents acting abroad. Offshore operations through such persons could fall outside the direct prohibition, although participating U.S. persons might still face liability.

12. **§ 3(a)—Unclear geographic reach.** “In the United States” is undefined, leaving questions about offshore waters, the exclusive economic zone, and activities aboard U.S.-flagged vessels outside U.S. territory. This particularly affects foreign persons not independently covered by the worldwide U.S.-person prohibition.

13. **§ 3(a)—Unclear coverage of supporting conduct.** “Engage in” does not expressly address financing, directing, contracting for, transporting, processing, or purchasing the output of mining. Some participation could be reached through ordinary criminal complicity rules, but the bill neither clearly prohibits all such support nor bans imports from otherwise uncovered foreign operations.

### Exceptions

14. **§ 3(b)—Broad, indefinite exploration-license grandfathering.** The exception exempts “mining” under a pre-enactment exploration license without an expiration date, production cap, or limit to previously conducted activity. Its breadth could allow continued mining insofar as the underlying license authorizes it; it does not itself enlarge that license’s authority.

15. **§ 3(b)—Unspecified licensing authority.** The bill does not identify which jurisdiction or agency must have issued the exploration license. Operators could argue that foreign or other licensing regimes qualify, rather than only a specified U.S. licensing program.

16. **§ 3(b)—Unclear treatment of transfers and modifications.** The exception does not address license transfers, renewals, amendments, enlarged operating areas, or successor licenses. Companies could seek to preserve grandfathered treatment while changing ownership or expanding operations.

17. **§ 3(c)—Environmental-assessment exception lacks limits.** There is no definition, prior approval requirement, independent oversight, quantity cap, or restriction on selling recovered material. An operator could characterize substantial extraction as environmental assessment, though merely applying that label would not necessarily establish the actual purpose.

18. **§ 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities are unresolved.** The exception does not require environmental assessment to be the sole or primary purpose. Mining undertaken partly for commercial reasons and partly to collect environmental data could therefore produce disputes about exemption eligibility.

### Registry and enforcement

19. **§§ 2(3), 4(a)—Registry coverage does not match prohibited mining.** Vessels of 5,000 gross tons or less need not register, even if their recovery exceeds the mining threshold. Equipment-based coverage also leaves questions about support vessels and distributed extraction systems.

20. **§ 4(a)—Undefined operator and jurisdictional scope.** The bill does not identify whether “operator” means the owner, charterer, manager, or another party. It also does not expressly limit registration to vessels with a U.S. connection, creating uncertainty about its intended foreign reach and enforceability.

21. **§ 4—Missing registration and reporting mechanics.** There is no registration deadline, requirement to register before recovery begins, or quarterly filing deadline. Reports need only “describe” recovery activities, without expressly providing tonnage, depth, location, license information, or a claimed exception.

22. **§ 4(b)—Reporting duty depends on registration.** The duty applies to “[e]ach registered operator,” rather than every operator required to register. An operator that never registers could argue it has not also violated the reporting requirement.

23. **§§ 4–5—No express penalties for registry violations.** Section 5 penalizes violations of § 3, not failures to register, failures to report, or inaccurate reports under § 4. Other laws might reach some false submissions, but the bill provides no clear, comprehensive sanction for registry noncompliance.

24. **§§ 3–5—No specified enforcement machinery.** The bill does not expressly assign investigative or civil-penalty assessment authority, establish an assessment procedure, or provide inspection, subpoena, audit, or record-retention powers. Existing governmental powers may fill some gaps, but the text leaves the enforcement route and means of verifying operator-certified reports unclear.

25. **§ 5—Limited express tools for stopping operations.** The bill supplies monetary penalties and criminal punishment but no express injunction, vessel detention, forfeiture, permit revocation, or restoration authority. Such measures might be available under other law, but they are not assured by this text.

26. **§ 5(b)—Willfulness and uncertain coverage.** Criminal liability requires a willful violation, making ambiguity about definitions, exceptions, and agency determinations particularly consequential. The precise meaning of “willfully” would require judicial interpretation; it should not be assumed that the government must always prove knowledge of this particular statute.

### Timing, international coverage, and termination

27. **§§ 5(a), 8—Conflicting commencement language.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while § 8 delays the Act’s effectiveness for 180 days. This creates avoidable uncertainty over civil liability during that interval; the bill should clearly align the prohibition and penalty start dates.

28. **§ 8—A 180-day transition window.** The delayed effective date allows otherwise lawful mining to continue before the prohibition takes effect. The exploration-license exception, however, uses the earlier enactment date, so licenses issued during that window are not clearly grandfathered.

29. **§ 6—No guaranteed international prohibition.** The Secretary of State must “seek to negotiate” an agreement, not secure one, and the deadline does not clearly distinguish beginning negotiations from completing them. This provision does not itself prohibit mining by foreign actors outside § 3’s jurisdiction or make any resulting agreement domestically enforceable.

30. **§ 7(a)—Unspecified harm standard and assessment process.** “Without serious harm” supplies no ecological benchmarks, geographic scale, time horizon, or treatment of cumulative effects. The bill also does not commission or fund the National Academies report, prescribe its contents, or specify how closely Congress’s finding must follow it.

31. **§ 7(a)—Unclear scope of early termination.** “The prohibition in section 3” ends upon the specified congressional action, but the registry and the rest of the Act apparently remain until sunset. The text does not explain this interim regime or expressly address liabilities and proceedings arising before termination.

32. **§ 7(b)—Unconditional ten-year sunset.** The entire Act expires after ten years regardless of whether Congress finds mining can occur without serious harm. This creates an independent route to resumed operations and ends the registry as well; the bill also leaves post-sunset treatment of pending enforcement and accrued liabilities to applicable saving rules rather than addressing it expressly.
